Big O notation is actually pretty approachable once you strip away the formal definitions. Let me break it down honestly.

## The core idea

Big O answers: **"As my input gets huge, how does my algorithm's work grow?"**

You're ignoring small inputs and constants because they don't matter at scale.

## Building intuition with concrete examples

**O(1)** - Looking up your name in a phone book if you know the exact page number. Doesn't matter if the book is 10 pages or 10,000 pages.

**O(n)** - You already get this. Reading every page once.

**O(n²)** - Comparing every person in a room to every other person. Double the people, quadruple the work.

## O(n log n) specifically

This trips people up because "log n" feels abstract.

Think of it this way: log n is roughly "how many times can I cut n in half before I reach 1?"
- 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 = 3 steps, and log₂(8) = 3

**So O(n log n) means:** you're doing that halving process, but for each of your n elements.

Merge sort is the classic example - you split your list in half repeatedly (the log n part), and at each level you process all n elements to merge them back together.

## Amortized analysis - where people genuinely get confused

This one actually requires a different mental model, so feeling lost here is reasonable, not dumb.

**The honest explanation:** Sometimes one operation is expensive, but it happens so rarely that if you average the cost across many operations, each one is cheap.

**Concrete example - dynamic arrays (like Python lists):**
- Usually adding an element is O(1) - just put it in the next slot
- But occasionally the array is full, so you copy everything to a bigger array - that's O(n)
- However, you doubled the size, so you won't need to copy again for n more insertions
- Spreading that O(n) cost across n operations = O(1) per operation on average

**That average cost is the amortized cost.**

## What your midterm probably actually tests

Be honest with yourself about what you're actually being asked:
- Identifying which category an algorithm falls into (usually more important than proving it formally)
- Comparing two algorithms
- Recognizing common patterns like nested loops = O(n²)

## A few things worth being clear about

The textbook formalism (with limits and formal proofs) is often harder than what you need for an intro midterm. If your professor emphasized the formal definition heavily, that matters. If they spent more time on practical analysis, focus there.

## Fibonacci complexity - you're correct on both

**Without memoization:** Yes, exponential - O(2^n) roughly. Here's why it's so bad:

To calculate fib(5), you calculate fib(4) and fib(3).
To calculate fib(4), you calculate fib(3) and fib(2).

Notice fib(3) gets calculated twice. fib(2) gets calculated even more times. The tree of redundant work explodes as n grows.

**With memoization:** Yes, O(n). The key insight is asking "how many unique subproblems are there?"

For fib(n), you only ever need fib(1), fib(2), fib(3)... fib(n). That's n unique calculations. After the first time you calculate each one, every future call just looks it up instantly. So you do n real calculations total.

**The general pattern for memoization complexity:**
> unique subproblems × work per subproblem

This works for most dynamic programming problems you'll see at this level.

## Why partitioning is O(n)

You nailed the intuition: you scan through the array once, and for each element you make one comparison against the pivot and put it in the right partition. One pass, n elements, O(n). That's it.

## Why pivot choice determines everything

This is the core insight for quicksort complexity. Think about what you actually want from a pivot.

**Best case - perfect pivot every time:**
Your pivot lands exactly in the middle, splitting the array in half each time. This gives you the same log n levels of recursion as merge sort, with O(n) work at each level. So O(n log n).

**Worst case - terrible pivot every time:**
Imagine your array is already sorted and you always pick the first element as pivot. The "smaller" partition has 0 elements, the "larger" partition has n-1 elements. You're not splitting, you're just peeling off one element at a time.

So instead of log n levels, you get n levels, each doing O(n) work. That's O(n²).

This is why sorted input can actually be quicksort's enemy, which feels counterintuitive.

**Average case:**
Here's the thing - truly terrible pivots are rare if you're picking randomly. Most pivots split the array "well enough" that on average you get O(n log n) behavior. This is why randomized quicksort is common in practice.

## The thing worth remembering for your exam

Merge sort is always O(n log n) - it's predictable. Quicksort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case - it's faster in practice but less predictable.

Your professor might ask you to compare them, and that tradeoff is usually what they're testing.

That said, here are the most common ways people accidentally tank Dijkstra's performance:

**The big one - not handling stale entries**
When you update a node's distance, many implementations just push a new entry to the priority queue rather than updating the existing one. This means your queue grows to O(E) entries instead of O(V). You end up processing the same node multiple times. The fix is checking when you pop a node whether the stored distance matches your current best distance, and skipping it if not.

**Rebuilding or rescanning the queue**
If you're doing something like calling sort() on a list instead of using a proper heap, or scanning for the minimum manually, that turns each extraction into O(V) instead of O(log V) and blows up your complexity.

**Adjacency matrix instead of adjacency list**
Like we talked about with BFS - if you're iterating through a full matrix row to find neighbors, you're adding V work per node instead of just the actual edges.

**Relaxing edges you don't need to**
If you're not skipping already-finalized nodes, you're doing redundant work.
